title: The Unlit Light of Eilean Mòr
summary: On Boxing Day 1900 the relief boat reaches the lonely Flannan Isles lighthouse and finds no one waiting: no flag, no smoke, no keepers. The light has been dark since the 15th. Inside, the house is tidy and cold, as if three careful men simply stepped out. Their echoes are still at their last tasks, each holding one piece of the last day. Across the island, the west landing shows what the sea did.

characters.name: Joseph Moore

art.description: Lean man of about thirty, clean-shaven pale face, damp dark hair under a navy wool keeper's cap with a brass badge, navy double-breasted pea jacket with brass buttons, thick grey knitted scarf, dark wool trousers, black rubber sea-boots, holding a lit brass hurricane lantern out in front
idle: standing still, lit lantern held out in the right hand, head tilted up

dialogue: A lighthouse is never quiet, miss. There's always somebody awake in it.
No flag on the staff. No empty boxes on the platform under the crane. They always leave the boxes.
Captain Harvie blew the whistle and fired a rocket. Not a soul came down.
The Archtor passed on the fifteenth and saw no light. That's eleven nights dark.
The crew must hold the boat off these rocks, and I can't leave them. Will you go up ahead of me?
The yard gate at the top of the brae will be shut. The spare key is in the red iron tool chest at the cliff foot, beside the crane.
The stair starts at the little gate there. I'll follow when the boat's secure.
afterwards: The red tool chest by the crane, miss. Then up the stair.
I'll follow as soon as I can.

examine: A roofless chapel of stacked stones, barely taller than a man. The old Blessing Chapel.
On the flat altar stone lie heaps of limpet shells and bent pins, left by generations of sheep-men.
They walked sunwise around it before they dared touch the island's grass.

The sheep-men sheltered here by day. Island custom said no one should spend a night on the Flannans.
They never did. The lighthouse men stayed every night.

characters.name: The Old Shepherd of Lewis

art.description: Tall stooped old man with a long white beard and deeply weathered brown face, dark blue knitted bonnet, long coat of undyed brown homespun wool belted with a rope, bare shins and rawhide shoes, leaning on a tall knotted wooden crook, pale and faintly translucent
idle: standing still, both hands resting on the top of the crook

dialogue: You came up without uncovering your head. Nobody teaches the young now.
My people grazed sheep here for a thousand years. We kept the old rules of the Flannans, and the island let us go home.
Bare your head on the grass. Walk sunwise round the chapel. Call nothing by its true name. And never stay the night.
The lighthouse men laughed at the rules. They stayed every night. Every single night.
When the sea is hungry, the Blue Men climb out of it, blue as slate and dripping. One walks the cliff path to the east now.
They are slow on dry ground. Keep moving and they cannot catch you.
The yard gate at the top of the slope is shut fast. The boatman's iron key will open it.
afterwards: Sunwise round the chapel, lass, and never stay the night.
Keep clear of the east edge. The Blue Man walks there.

characters.name: Thomas Marshall

art.description: Lean man around thirty with a sandy moustache and pale freckled face, ochre-yellow oilskin coat and trousers streaming with seawater, black sou'wester tied under the chin, black rubber sea-boots, a coil of tarred rope over one shoulder, whole figure tinted faint grey-blue
idle: standing still facing forward, rope coil on the left shoulder, water running from the coat hem

dialogue: Is that the relief? You're early, or I'm late. I only came in for my boots.
That storm on the fourteenth threw spray clean over the west cliff. I never saw the like.
Mr Ducat's not slept easy since. The crane ropes are kept in a wooden box wedged in a crack above the west landing.
One more sea like that and the Board loses the lot.
I lost gear to a gale once. Five shillings they fined me. I'll not pay for the Board's gear twice.
The store room? It's locked. The principal keeps his spare key in his sea chest.
The oak one with the brass corners, at the foot of the first bed, by the window.
Now pardon me. They'll be waiting on me at the crane.
afterwards: The brass-cornered chest, miss, by the window. I've the crane to see to.

characters.name: James Ducat, principal keeper

art.description: Stocky bearded man in his forties, dark beard flecked grey and crusted with white salt, ruddy face, open ochre-yellow oilskin coat over navy tunic with brass buttons, black sou'wester pushed back, black sea-boots, chalk and small brass key in hands, faint grey-blue tint, water dripping
idle: standing still, chalk raised in the right hand, brass key held in the left

dialogue: Is that the relief? You'll be wanting the log. It's written up, never fear.
Slate's done to nine this morning. Wind easing, sea still heavy. The fair copy can wait till tonight.
On the fourteenth the sea came up that west cliff like a man climbing stairs.
It near tore the rope box out of its crevice above the west landing. Marshall and I are going down to lash it before the next sea does.
Lamp's trimmed, oil's in, lens is clean. I'll light her at dusk, same as always.
Go up the tower and see for yourself. Here, take the tower key.
The west gate key is up in the lamp room, in the tin of lens cloths in the small white cupboard by the stair hatch.
Shut the gate behind you when you go through. The sheep get in.
afterwards: The lamp's ready. Go up and see, miss.
West gate key's in the lens-cloth tin, up in the lamp room.

characters.name: Donald MacArthur

art.description: Broad-shouldered young man, black hair plastered flat with seawater, strong square face, mouth open shouting, soaked collarless white linen shirt with sleeves rolled to the elbow, dark wool waistcoat, braces, grey wool trousers, black boots, whole figure pale grey-blue with water running off him
idle: standing still, right arm raised high and pointing forward

dialogue: Is it lit? Tell me the light is lit!
I was at the top of the stair when I saw it. A sea standing up out of the west, higher than the cliff.
Ducat and Marshall were down at the crane, lashing the rope box, with their backs to it.
I had no time for my oilskins. I ran down in my shirt, shouting, and the wind tore the words out of my mouth.
They turned just as it came. It took all three of us off this rock.
No murder, no madness, miss. Only the sea, and three men down here to save the Board's gear.
I laughed at the old tales of the Blue Men. But that is what the sea looks like when it comes for you.
Then it was cold, and dark, and quiet, the way it has been ever since. Someone must light the light.

characters.name: A Blue Man of the Minch

art.description: Tall thin man-shaped figure with smooth slate-blue skin, long grey-green hair hanging in wet ropes like kelp, bare chest, sodden blue-grey sailcloth wrapped from the waist down, long webbed fingers, pale milky white eyes, brown bladderwrack strands on his shoulders, water streaming off him
idle: standing still, long arms hanging at his sides
moving: mid-stride, left leg forward, webbed hands reaching forward
mid-stride, right leg forward, webbed hands reaching forward

dialogue: Up the stair and over the stone; the sea came calling, the sea went home.

characters.name: A second Blue Man of the Minch

art.description: Short hunched man-shaped figure with mottled slate-blue skin, tangle of dark olive kelp hair hanging over his face, ragged grey-blue sailcloth wrap with a frayed rope belt, long webbed hands with black nails, white barnacles crusting his shoulders, water dripping from his fingers
moving: hunched mid-stride, left leg forward, hands swinging low
hunched mid-stride, right leg forward, hands swinging low

dialogue: Three went down where the cold ropes lie.
